title: Code Preview And A Lighter Issue Rule
eyebrow: Design for approval · two changes to the design loop · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: code preview and issue rule

short.lead: Today a build plan says which files each step touches and roughly how many lines, but you never see the lines themselves until the build is done. With this change, every step in a build plan carries the actual code I intend to write, shown as a diff against today's code. You read it, change it, and only then type "Build plan approved". A habit you don't want, such as a swallowed error or a value quietly reset, is caught on the page instead of in a pull request. Separately, a build plan will need only one issue. When two or more steps are large, each large step also gets its own sub-issue.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what it creates and what it needs from you.
items: During the Plan stage I write each step's planned code as a diff file (a list of added and removed lines) in the repo, before any source file is touched.
The build plan shows the code
The page builder (make_page.py) gets a new plan mode. It shows each step's draft on the build plan page as a readable diff, and each file opens when you tap it.
Your changes go into the drafts, and the page is rebuilt so you approve exactly what will be built.
You read each step's code and say what to change, or approve it.

One issue, sub-issues for large steps
A small feature needs one issue. A feature with two or more large steps gets one main issue plus one sub-issue per large step.
Nothing from you, unless you disagree with which steps I marked large.

changes: new
Code drafts, one diff file per step
The planned code, written where you can read and edit it.

During Plan I write each step's code as a unified diff against the current branch, at docs/plans/<feature>-code/<step>.diff. The code lock blocks source edits outside Build, but files under docs/ stay editable, so drafting needs no exception to the lock, and no source file changes until you approve. A new file shows as all added lines. An edit also shows the unchanged lines around it, so you can see where it lands.
Nothing shows the code before it is written. A build plan lists files and estimated line counts only.
A folder of diff files, one per step, committed with the plan.
You see every line before it exists, and you can edit a draft directly if you'd rather not describe the change.

Plan mode in the page builder
make_page.py renders the drafts on the build plan page.

A plan block in the page's content file (the .page.json) names each step's draft. The builder reads each diff and shows it per file, with added and removed lines marked. It refuses a step that names no draft, or a draft that doesn't apply to the current code. It records the page's path in the design loop's stage file as the plan page, the way QA mode already records the QA page.
make_page.py has a QA mode and a sweep mode, and no plan mode.

The "Build plan approved" gate
It also waits for a fresh, linked plan page.
"Build plan approved" needs at least two labelled issues, every issue in progress, and a new decisions-log entry.
It also needs the plan page from plan mode, linked in a reply, and built after the last edit to any draft. If you edit a draft, the page is rebuilt before your approval counts.

The builder hand-off
The builder is told to apply the approved draft.
The builder gets the step and its issue, and writes the code itself.
The builder gets the step's approved draft as its specification. Where the real code has to differ, it makes the change and reports it with the reason, never silently.

The QA page compares planned code with real code.

The issue requirement
One issue is enough unless the work has several large steps.

Every build plan needs at least two labelled issues, a parent and a child, before "Build plan approved" counts. Separately, any plan with more than three numbered lines blocks code edits until two issues exist.

Every build plan needs one labelled issue. When two or more steps are marked large, it also needs one sub-issue per large step, each saying "Part of" the main issue. Small steps never need their own issue.

Both checks read one number, ISSUES_NEEDED in house_rules/design_loop.py, which is 2 today. That number is replaced by the rule above. Which steps count as large is the choice below called "Who decides that a step is large?". Risks and unknowns
What could make this cost more than it saves.

Planning takes longer, because the code is written twice: once as a draft and once for real. That cost is unmeasured; milestone 4 measures it on one small feature. Large steps make long pages; each file opens on tap to keep the page readable. Drafts can go stale if main moves during Plan; plan mode refuses a draft that no longer applies, so a stale draft is redone, not built on.
No risk today, because no code is shown.
Longer planning and longer plan pages.
You trade some speed in Plan for catching problems before they are built.
new
Milestones
Five checks, each one you can run or look at yourself.

Milestones 1, 2, 3 and 5 each pass when their new verify.py cases pass. 1. make_page.py in plan mode renders a sample diff, and refuses a step without a draft and a draft that doesn't apply. 2. "Build plan approved" is refused with no plan page, with an unlinked page, and with a page older than a draft, and accepted with a fresh linked page. 3. A QA page built from a build that departs from its draft lists that departure, and one that only reformats lists none. 4. One small real feature goes through Design, Plan with code, Build and QA, with screenshots of its plan page at phone width in light and dark, and the extra Plan time noted. 5. A plan with one small step is approved with one issue, and a plan with two large steps is refused until it has a main issue and two sub-issues.
No milestones exist for this.
Five checkable milestones.
You can see when each part is done.
choices: detail
How much code should each step's preview show?
A
Every line, as a diff
The full planned change for every file, so nothing is hidden in a body you didn't see.
B
Signatures and short sketches
Each function's name and inputs, with a few lines of plain description for its body. Faster, but a swallowed error lives in the body.
C
Full code for risky parts only
Every line for error handling, file writes and anything destructive; signatures for the rest. I decide which parts are risky.

You want to curb specific habits before they ship, and those habits live in individual lines: an `except` that hides a failure, a silent default, a fallback nobody asked for. Only the full diff shows them reliably.
strict
How closely must the build follow the approved draft?
A
Follow it; report every departure
The builder may differ from the draft where the real code demands it, and every difference appears on the QA page with its reason.
B
Refuse departures until you approve them
A hook stops the build at any difference until you approve it. Tightest, but it stalls on small things.
C
Guidance only
The draft informs the build; differences are not tracked.
A strict match breaks on harmless things such as a renamed local variable, and would stop the build for each one. Reporting every difference keeps you in control without stopping work.
edits
How do you send changes to the code?
A
Say it in your reply, or edit the draft file
Describe the change in chat, or edit docs/plans/<feature>-code/ yourself. Either way I update the draft and rebuild the page.
B
Edit the code on the page
Each code view is an editable box, and your edits are copied into your reply as a diff. Better on a phone, but adds a code editor to every page.
C
Reply only
You describe changes in chat; the draft files are mine alone.
A reply works from your phone, and editing the file works at a desk. Both already exist, so nothing new has to be built for them.
large
Who decides that a step is large?
A
I mark it on the plan page; you can overrule
Each step on the build plan page says Large or Small. The page builder records how many are large, and the gate counts from that.
B
A size rule decides
A step is large when its planned code passes a line count, such as 100 lines. Measurable, but art steps such as building rigs have no code to count.
C
You say it each time
You name the large steps in your reply before I create the issues.
Your guards example is mostly art and animation work, where a line count means nothing. Marking each step on the page lets you see and correct the call before any issue is made.

wrapup.summary: Every build plan step will carry the actual code I intend to write, shown as a diff you can change before approving. The approval waits for that code, the builder follows it, and QA shows where the real code differs. A build plan also needs only one issue. Sub-issues are added only when two or more steps are large.
wrapup.changing: The Plan stage gains code drafts and a plan page that shows them. The "Build plan approved" gate, the builder hand-off and QA mode are adapted. The two-issue minimum becomes one issue, with sub-issues only when two or more steps are large. Nothing else is removed.
wrapup.blocking: Nothing is built until you approve this design.
wrapup.next: After you approve, I write the systems doc and the issues under the new rule, then bring the build plan. That build plan will be the first one to carry its own code preview, with its code drafted by hand, since plan mode won't exist yet.
